1:59 Hey that's my town!

I live in Valdez, Alaska. I'm always happy to brag about it so here's some interesting stuff:

It’s home to more wild animals than you can shake a stick at. This includes, black bears, grizzly bears, moose, big horn (Dall) sheep, mountain goats, Sitka black-tailed deer, caribou, seals, sea lions, sea otters, and various whales and porpoises, such as humpback whales and orcas. If you like game fish, Valdez is home to gigantic halibut, salmon (king, pink, silver, sockeye, and chum), rockfish, and lingcod. Freshwater options include trout and Dolly Varden. As for the birds, puffins (horned and tufted), kittiwakes, and trumpeter swans can be found everywhere. Common year-round species include bald eagles and magpies, while summer brings migratory birds like arctic terns, kingfishers, and various waterfowl like harlequin ducks. There are so many bald eagles here that they swarm like pigeons in Central Park. They can be a real nuisance when trying to clean your fish at the local docks, but they are truly amazing to watch.

Unfortunately, Valdez was the principle victim of the Valdez oil spill in 1989. Although mostly recovered, there are still a few remote island spots where oil blobs foul the coast. But pretty much everything is thriving now. 

Valdez is located in a coastal temperate rainforest. This is the most northerly extensions of the Pacific temperate rainforest system and sits among the Chugach Mountains. It’s one of the snowiest places on earth, averaging about 330 inches of snow every year. That’s in addition to the 85 inches of rainfall. Valdez is surrounded by five major glaciers. It was founded as a gateway to the interior of Alaska during the Klondike gold rush. It’s now the southern terminal of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System (TAPS).

Valdez has one more claim to fame. On Friday, March 27, 1964, (Good Friday) at 5:36 p.m. local time (Alaska Standard Time), Valdez was hit with a 9.2 megathrust earthquake. The epicenter The epicenter was located in Prince William Sound, west-southwest of Valdez. The Great Alaska Earthquake as it is sometimes called was the largest recorded earthquake in North American history and the second most powerful in world history. 

 The intense shaking, which lasted for over four minutes, triggered a massive underwater landslide at the Valdez waterfront. Millions of cubic yards of earth and the entire waterfront area — including docks, warehouses, and canneries — slid into the bay. The landslide generated a local tsunami that surged into the town within minutes, destroying the remaining structures and the entire fishing fleet. The largest wave run-up in the Valdez Inlet was recorded at 220 feet (67 m) in Shoup Bay. In Valdez alone, 32 people died, primarily due to the waterfront collapse and the local tsunami. Most fatalities across all affected areas were caused by tsunamis rather than the ground shaking itself. Ruptured oil tanks ignited a massive fire, adding to the destruction.

 The original town site was built on unstable sand and gravel that was prone to liquefaction and vulnerable to future tsunamis. Consequently, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and urban renewal funds were used to relocate the entire town to its present, more stable location on the Mineral Creek fan, 4 miles away from the original site. The relocation and rebuilding process took several years to complete. 

So if you’re into outdoor activities, come on up! It’s beautiful up here!
